episode_title: You Should Start a Business: Part 2

stories.topic: Musk Prices a Battery From Scratch
stories.summary: Experts said batteries couldn't get much cheaper. Market forces and the best scientists had already done their work, so only small gains were left. Musk broke a battery down into its material constituents. He worked out how much of each went into a pack, what each cost on the spot markets and what assembly cost. By the time of the interview he had cut costs from $600 to $80 per kilowatt hour. Amit contrasts this with Ajay's advice, in an earlier episode, to respect experts in complicated fields.
stories.insight: Conventional wisdom is often a stale snapshot. Either it took a limited view, or it was right once and the world moved on. Rebuilding a problem from its raw ingredients is how you catch that lag, and Amit argues all progress comes from doing so.
stories.quote: And by doing this, he figured out that the conventional thinking was BS.

stories.topic: Larry Page Demos PageRank to Excite
stories.summary: Aravind Srinivas recalls a Larry Page interview. Page tried to sell his PageRank technology to Excite, then one of the big search engines. In the demo, searching 'university' with his tech brought up Harvard and Stanford, while Excite returned random junk. The Excite executive said nobody types 'university'; a proper user would ask for the best Ivy League university in America. Page said that was blaming the user. Years later, Srinivas's mother complained that Perplexity wasn't giving her what she wanted. He was about to tell her to fix the grammar of her question, then stopped himself.
stories.insight: When users struggle, saying 'you're using it wrong' is the founder's Kool-Aid talking. The customer's confusion is feedback on the product, not a flaw in the customer.
stories.quote: You're gaslighting the user. You're saying the user is stupid. The user is not searching properly. The problem is not with the user, the problem is with you.

stories.topic: Phil Knight and the Guy Under the Lamp Post
stories.summary: Simon Sinek recalls a conference where Phil Knight asked everyone who runs to stand. He then asked people to sit down in stages: first those who don't run weekly, then those who don't run twice a week. Finally only those who run three times a week, rain or shine, whether they feel good or bad, were left standing, just a handful. Knight told them that the next time they are out before dawn, wet and miserable and still running, the guy under the lamp post cheering them on is Nike.
stories.insight: 'Just Do It' is about doing, not winning. A brand that stands beside your perseverance is selling a story about who you are, not sneakers.
stories.quote: the next time that you are out there before dawn running in the darkness and it's wet and you're feeling miserable and you're still running. You know, if there's a guy under the lamp post who is cheering you on, that's us.

stories.topic: Bill Gates Pulled the Radio Out of His Car
stories.summary: Mike Moritz was being driven to the airport by Bill Gates, probably in the early eighties by Amit's guess. He noticed the slot where the car radio should be was empty and asked if it had been stolen. Gates said he had taken it out himself. Amit pairs this with Jensen Huang, who doesn't wear a watch because 'now is the most important time.'
stories.insight: Obsession in practice means designing distractions out of your life. Amit borrows Apoorva Mehta's definition: the company is the last thing you think about at night and the first thing in the morning.
stories.quote: No, no, no, no one stole it, I took it out. Because if I listen to the radio, that'll take away my time for thinking about Microsoft.

stories.topic: BillDesk's Three Founders in One Room
stories.summary: Ajay's friend Ajay Kaushal co-founded BillDesk, a very successful Indian firm. Its big exit got snarled up by Indian government delays; otherwise it would have been one of the biggest exits in Indian history. Its three co-founders sit in one room and argue over every important decision together, and none of them wants to be sole CEO. They did this with zero employees and still do it with ten thousand. Ajay credits Kaushal's quiet, unassuming, idea-first character. Amit calls it an outlier, but a lesson to think for yourself rather than follow 'have one CEO' as a hard rule.
stories.insight: Founder structure can follow temperament rather than template. Humility plus genuine interest in the argument can make shared leadership work where ego would break it.
stories.quote: So they think none of us is good enough to do it alone.

stories.topic: Nonstop Dan's Phantom Vegan Meal on Air India
stories.summary: Nonstop Dan pays his own way to review business and first class, and Amit has twice picked an airline on his advice. Dan praised Air India's new business class: higher walls, more privacy, a door you can close. But his pre-ordered special meal (vegan, Amit thinks) was never loaded. The crew insisted the regular menu dish, with cheese in it, was his vegan meal. A superior came over and seemed just as lost, and the same thing happened at the second meal. Amit's right answer: apologise, admit the meal was forgotten, offer options from other cabins, and make it up to him afterwards.
stories.insight: This is Bezos's 'optimise for truth-telling' in miniature. The reflex to cover up rather than admit ignorance can be dangerous in service, and Amit sees the same habit in people who give street directions they don't actually know.
stories.quote: What if I had a food allergy? What if I said I'm allergic to peanuts and there were peanuts in something? And not only did these people not know it, they lied to me about it.

stories.topic: Stripe Turned a Seven-Day Integration Into Five Minutes
stories.summary: When e-commerce was taking off, integrating PayPal into a website took about seven days and a hundred-page manual, sometimes with a dedicated team. Stripe, chasing its mission to 'increase the GDP of the internet', stripped out every unnecessary feature and process. You paste a snippet of embed code, test it once, and you're done. Amit has seen this himself while setting up payments for his courses.
stories.insight: Simplicity is subtraction. A grand mission becomes concrete through the ruthless removal of friction for the user.
stories.quote: You take a little piece of embed code, you put it on your webpage, and then it just shows and you test it once, and it is done in five minutes.

stories.topic: Bezos's 30-Page Plan He Knew Was BS
stories.summary: Bezos wrote a 30-page business plan for Amazon to show investors. He knew it would fall apart on contact with reality, and so did the VCs. Amit pairs it with Mike Tyson's line about everyone having a plan until they get punched in the face.
stories.insight: The plan is worthless but the planning is not. Writing at length about the future forces long-term, clarified thinking. The same logic underlies Eric Schmidt's case for five-year plans inside firms.
stories.quote: But that exercise of writing thirty pages is important because it clarifies your thinking.

stories.topic: The Founder Who Turned His Hires Into Co-Founders
stories.summary: A friend of the hosts started a company in Bangalore as more or less a solopreneur. He then hired a CTO and one other person. He was so impressed by their commitment, insight and passion that he gave them equal shares and made them co-founders. Amit notes you don't have to go that far, since there are other ways to reward early employees.
stories.insight: The people worth hiring are those who already act like owners. They question the task, suggest better ways, and tell the founder when he's wrong.
stories.quote: you are showing as much ownership as I am, so it is only fair that you are co founders.

stories.topic: Amit Discovers He Works Like a Lion
stories.summary: In Eisenhower's matrix, Amit has long lamented living in two quadrants: 'not important, not urgent' or 'important and urgent' (deadlines, shoots, releases). He rarely reaches 'important, not urgent', where reading and learning happen. Tim Urban wrote about the same dilemma. Naval Ravikant's 'work like a lion' reframed it for him. A lion sleeps most of the day and then sprints for the kill, and humans shaped in the hunter-gatherer age are similar. Focus burns calories, so distraction conserves energy for the hunt. His fix is to accept the wiring and use hacks like calendarising to turn important-not-urgent tasks into urgent ones.
stories.insight: Seeing a 'flaw' as evolved hardware removes the moral shame and points to practical workarounds. This is the Life Lessons idea of amplifying good wiring and mitigating bad wiring.
stories.quote: So it is natural for us, it is efficient for us, it is rational for us to get distracted because we save the calories for the hunt.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Recapped at the top of this episode. Amit asks viewers to watch it, and at the end to 'watch these two episodes again'.
recommendations.reason: It sets up this episode. It covers being inward-driven, the project-to-product-to-business path, getting a few people to love your product, ignoring naysayers, and the bias for action.

recommendations.item: Sam Altman on being a generalist
recommendations.creator: Sam Altman
recommendations.reason: Altman argues you can be a specialist while it's a project, but the moment you become a company founder you must step back and think broadly.

recommendations.creator: Elon Musk
recommendations.context: Chapter 2: Musk explains how he thinks about battery packs.
recommendations.reason: It is a concrete example of pricing materials from scratch, which took battery costs from $600 to $80 per kWh against expert consensus.

recommendations.item: Aravind Srinivas speaks of Larry Page
recommendations.creator: Aravind Srinivas
recommendations.reason: It tells the Larry Page and Excite story, and how it stopped Srinivas from blaming his own mother's search phrasing. Never blame the user.

recommendations.creator: Garry Tan
recommendations.context: Chapter 3. Tan describes how, at his pre-Y Combinator startup, the CEO personally answered customer complaints one day a week.
recommendations.reason: Small companies shouldn't imitate big-company polish. Smallness lets you get close to every customer.

recommendations.creator: Kevin Hale
recommendations.context: Chapter 4. Amit calls the quote one he loves.
recommendations.reason: 'Marketing is a tax you pay for not making your product awesome' captures Amit's product-first philosophy.

recommendations.creator: Jeff Bezos
recommendations.reason: Bezos describes how, over his lifetime, the focus has shifted from marketing to product. Build something great and word of mouth spreads it.

recommendations.creator: Naval Ravikant
recommendations.reason: Networking is personal marketing. Do great work and your network forms around you, which matches Amit's experience with his podcasts.

recommendations.creator: Jeff Bezos
recommendations.context: Chapter 5. Bezos recalls being inspired by reading about Sony in the 1980s.
recommendations.reason: Morita's mission, 'make Japan known for quality again', is a model of a purpose bigger than the product.

recommendations.creator: Patrick Collison
recommendations.reason: 'Increase the GDP of the internet' is another mission bigger than the company itself.

recommendations.creator: Simon Sinek
recommendations.context: Chapter 5. Sinek retells Phil Knight's 'guy under the lamp post' speech.
recommendations.reason: It shows a brand built on 'we are with you when you do', not on selling shoes. Amit says it moves him.

recommendations.creator: Jensen Huang
recommendations.reason: Huang wasn't trying to be a big fish in a small pond but to enlarge the pond, creating new markets instead of fighting over old ones.

recommendations.creator: Sam Altman
recommendations.reason: 'A long term commitment is the only arbitrage opportunity left in the market' when everyone else chases the next quarter.

recommendations.creator: Jeff Bezos
recommendations.reason: Plans fall apart on contact with reality, but writing them clarifies your thinking and pushes you to look ahead.

recommendations.creator: Vinod Khosla
recommendations.reason: 'Be obstinate about your vision, but flexible about your tactics' shows how long-term vision and daily adaptation coexist.

recommendations.creator: Eric Schmidt
recommendations.context: Chapter 6. Amit notes the irony given India's failed planning era.
recommendations.reason: An economy can't be centrally planned but a company can. A five-year plan forces you to imagine the world ahead and where you'll need to pivot.

recommendations.item: Everything is Everything episodes on firms (incl. Family Firms; Imperial vs Decentralised Firms)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit flags them explicitly as a recommendation while discussing boards. Ajay later cites the imperial-firms episode.
recommendations.reason: They go deeper on independent boards and on why information fails to flow in large, imperial firms.

recommendations.creator: Patrick Collison
recommendations.context: Chapter 7. Collison co-founded Stripe with his brother John.
recommendations.reason: Starting a company with someone you're close to is a feature, not a bug.

recommendations.creator: Brian Chesky
recommendations.reason: You'll spend more time with your co-founder than your spouse, and 'winning an argument is not as important as preserving the relationship'. Amit sees this as key to his partnership with Ajay.

recommendations.creator: Naval Ravikant
recommendations.reason: Look for high intelligence, high energy and high integrity, and integrity matters most by far.

recommendations.creator: Garry Tan
recommendations.reason: Co-CEOs may suit the founders but slow every decision for everyone below them. Have one decision-maker.

recommendations.creator: Paul Graham
recommendations.reason: Ten random rowers make an average boat; the ten best make a much faster one.

recommendations.creator: Steve Jobs
recommendations.reason: Everything depends on your first five hires. A-list people attract other A-list people, and that becomes the culture.

recommendations.creator: Sam Altman
recommendations.reason: Hire for values first, aptitude second, skill third.

recommendations.item: Mike Moritz on Bill Gates's car radio
recommendations.creator: Mike Moritz
recommendations.reason: Gates removed his car radio so he could think about Microsoft. It is a vivid picture of founder obsession.

recommendations.item: Huang on not wearing a watch
recommendations.creator: Jensen Huang
recommendations.reason: 'Now is the most important time.' Give whatever you're doing your full attention.

recommendations.creator: Sam Altman
recommendations.reason: Hard work doesn't burn you out, because momentum is energising. Amit thinks burnout comes more from worry, procrastination and overthinking.

recommendations.creator: Jeff Bezos
recommendations.reason: Bezos rejects 'work-life balance' for 'work-life harmony': go where the energy is.

recommendations.creator: Jensen Huang
recommendations.reason: Greatness involves suffering. Huang doesn't feel joy about his company every day, but he feels love, and love drives the hard work.

recommendations.item: Ravikant on working like a lion
recommendations.creator: Naval Ravikant
recommendations.reason: Lions rest most of the time and then sprint. It helped Amit accept his own burst-driven way of working.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit says Naval's lion idea ties in with what they teach in the course.
recommendations.reason: The course covers how our hunter-gatherer wiring clashes with modern life, and how to amplify the good and mitigate the bad.

recommendations.creator: Tim Urban
recommendations.reason: Urban writes about exactly Amit's dilemma: living in the urgent or the trivial quadrants and never reaching the important-but-not-urgent one.

recommendations.creator: Jeff Bezos
recommendations.reason: Humans evolved to get along, not to tell the truth, so companies must deliberately build mechanisms and a culture of truth-telling.

recommendations.creator: Lex Fridman
recommendations.reason: Here Bezos explains 'disagree and commit': argue, then fully own the decision without any 'I told you so' later.

recommendations.creator: Nonstop Dan
recommendations.context: Chapter 10. A reviewer Amit trusts enough to have chosen airlines by.
recommendations.reason: It is a live example of a crew lying about a missing special meal instead of owning the mistake.

recommendations.creator: Vlad Tenev
recommendations.reason: 'One screen, one button, one action' guards against throwing every good idea into the product.

recommendations.creator: Patrick Collison
recommendations.reason: People like beautiful things. Beauty and simplicity go together and are worth aiming for even when hard to quantify.

recommendations.creator: Jeff Bezos
recommendations.reason: 99% of your work will never be seen, so take pride in it anyway.

recommendations.creator: Warren Buffett
recommendations.reason: Buffett's father taught him to live by his inner scorecard of values rather than the outer scorecard of money and reputation.

recommendations.item: How Will You Measure Your Life?
recommendations.creator: Clayton Christensen et al.
recommendations.context: Ajay's recommendation, 'directly flowing' from the inner-scorecard chapter. Amit adds: 'It's a beautiful, simple book. Everybody should read it.'
recommendations.reason: It extends the idea of judging your life by your own values rather than external success.

recommendations.creator: Startup Archive
recommendations.context: The Instagram account where Amit found most of this episode's founder clips.
recommendations.reason: It collects the views of founders whom Amit counts among today's finest thinkers.

recommendations.creator: Paul Graham
recommendations.context: Amit's closing recommendation, given before and repeated here.
recommendations.reason: Graham takes months over each essay and gathers feedback from friends. The essays are models of simple, elegant, clear writing, and offer frameworks for life and humanity, not just business.

recommendations.context: Show-notes link for the opening riff, where Amit 'translates' the Bollywood song 'Sarkai Lo Khatiya Jaada Lage' into a liberaliser's slogan.
recommendations.reason: It is the comic set-piece that opens the episode.

core_ideas.concept: Specialist for the Project, Generalist for the Company
core_ideas.explanation: Following Sam Altman, Amit says a project can be driven by deep specialism, as Page and Brin's PageRank was. Once it becomes a company, the founder must step back and think broadly. Ajay adds that missions like 'organise the world's information' open you to adjacencies, and warns that VCs often try to keep founders tied to the last pitch deck. Amit recalls Vinod Khosla's claim that most VCs add negative value, which puts the burden on founders to do their own learning.
core_ideas.quote: What do they know of England who only England knows? said Rudyard Kipling, what do they know of cricket who only cricket knows, said C. L. R. James.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues that the highest-level work in any firm is strategy: who are we, what are our capabilities, what amazing things can we do that the world will like? Execution orders flow down from that. Leaders must keep re-evaluating and changing their minds, so thinking like a founder makes even employees better.
core_ideas.quote: So when you're an employee, you're being told to shut up, be narrow, execute, execute, execute. But at the leadership level, it's upside down.

core_ideas.explanation: Don't inherit assumptions; rebuild the problem from its fundamentals. Conventional thinking lags reality. Sometimes it took a limited view, sometimes it was right once and the world changed.
core_ideas.quote: All progress happens because someone challenged the conventional thinking and on some margin the conventional thinking was wrong.

core_ideas.concept: Obsess Over Customers, Not Competitors, and Act Small
core_ideas.explanation: Start inward-driven, but once the business exists the customer is everything. Bezos ignored competitors and focused on what won't change: people will always want lower prices, better value and faster delivery. Never blame the user for your product's failures. Garry Tan adds: when you're small, act small. Don't mimic big-company polish; use your size to talk to every customer.
core_ideas.quote: smallness is a luxury that allows you to get that intimacy with your customer and build an incredible product.

core_ideas.explanation: A great product spreads by word of mouth, and your tribe will find you. Amit admits there may be an optimum of 5–10% marketing, but he won't spend bandwidth finding it. The real danger is that a marketing mindset takes over your thinking and pulls you toward the lowest common denominator and short-term gratification. Naval applies the same logic to people: networking is personal marketing, so do great work instead.
core_ideas.quote: And the quote is marketing is a tax you pay for not making your product awesome.

core_ideas.explanation: Examples include Sony ('make Japan known for quality again'), Google ('organise the world's information'), Stripe ('increase the GDP of the internet'), Nike (be with people when they do, not only when they win) and NVIDIA (grow the pond instead of fighting in it). A big mission keeps you energised. Ajay adds that it also shapes recruitment: narrow bean-counter firms attract average people, while audacious ones attract remarkable people, as Apple's love of beauty attracted the best designers.
core_ideas.quote: Whereas the firms that go after big audacious dreams are more likely to get remarkable people joining.

core_ideas.concept: Long-Term Commitment as the Last Arbitrage
core_ideas.explanation: When everyone optimises for the next quarter, thinking in decades is your edge, and it attracts a different calibre of people. Hold the vision firmly but change tactics daily as reality pushes back. Plans, whether Bezos's 30 pages or Schmidt's five years, matter for the thinking they force, not the document.
core_ideas.quote: a long term commitment is the only arbitrage opportunity left in the market.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay notes that bosses preach long-term thinking while HR pays bonuses on narrow, one-quarter KPIs, which teaches people to shut up and execute. He calls short-termism the bane of India. His fix is to speak in compounding numbers that excite people, like 5x in five years or 10x in ten. That pushes managers to ask what a ten-times bigger firm needs and to invest in the foundations of growth, instead of squeezing a bit more profit from existing capabilities.
core_ideas.quote: That if you think your people are very short sighted, it's your fault.

core_ideas.concept: The Glory of Capitalism Is in Large Firms
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues that the top twenty thousand non-financial firms essentially are the Indian economy. Scale buys the resources for subtle refinements of product, process and productivity. The puzzle is keeping a small firm's hunger, imagination and strategic thinking once you have ten thousand people. Amit counters with Naval's vision of tiny teams doing what giant firms do. Ajay replies that this will hold in a few industries, but operations like Britannia's will always be vast and complex.
core_ideas.quote: So all the glory of modern capitalism is actually in the large companies.

core_ideas.explanation: You'll spend more time with your co-founder than your spouse, so closeness is an asset. Look for intelligence, energy and above all integrity. Preserve the relationship over winning arguments. Prefer a single CEO so decisions don't stall, but treat even that as a default to reason about, not a law.
core_ideas.quote: winning an argument is not as important as preserving the relationship.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's addition: the best partnerships bring different knowledge and viewpoints, and both people update on each other's evidence (Bayesian updating). The point of arguing isn't the single decision but jointly building a better theory of the world and of the firm, so later decisions keep improving. People too sure of themselves to update have a serious character flaw.
core_ideas.quote: And the purpose of the disagreement actually is to build a model of the world.

core_ideas.concept: Hire A-Players for Values, Not Credentials
core_ideas.explanation: Hire for values first, aptitude second, skill third. A-list people pick what excites them over the best salary, and they attract more A-list people. Hire people who think like co-founders, and don't fear hiring people smarter than you. Ajay's caution: 'best' means knowledge, character and connection with the world, not IIT or IIM badges.
core_ideas.quote: when Amit says the best people, the A-list people, he does not mean the credentialed ones.

core_ideas.explanation: Mandated 70-hour weeks are wrong, but there's no route to excellence without hard work you choose. Momentum energises; Amit thinks burnout comes more from worrying, procrastinating and overthinking. Aim for work-life harmony and go where the energy is. Huang's distinction is that work won't always bring joy, but love for the mission sustains it.
core_ideas.quote: But the path to excellence always comes with hard work. That's non-negotiable.

core_ideas.explanation: We evolved as social animals to get along, and in a tribe a truth-teller could be clubbed to death. So by default organisations drift toward deference up the hierarchy and politeness among peers. Firms must build mechanisms against this, like Bezos's 'disagree and commit'. Amit links failures like Kodak, which sat on digital photography, partly to truth not travelling upward.
core_ideas.quote: We've evolved to get along with each other. Right? We've not evolved to tell the truth.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay calls information the central crisis of firms. Knowledge about customers in each locale and the best way to produce there exists inside the firm, but in large 'imperial' firms it doesn't bubble up. A top team convinced it has the one right answer for the whole world pushes orders down and stops listening, and productivity suffers.
core_ideas.quote: But the imperium that firms build inside themselves hinders those information flows.

core_ideas.explanation: Examples include Robinhood's one screen, one button, one action and Stripe's five-minute integration. SpaceX's Raptor 3 looked like a toy next to the 'Christmas tree' Raptor 1, yet was lighter and more powerful. A pen design has gone unchanged since 1955, and Picasso's bulls were distilled to a few lines. Beauty travels with simplicity: Amit, once an Apple sceptic, now concedes the value of its aesthetic.
core_ideas.quote: The evolution to greatness is always an evolution towards simplicity.

core_ideas.explanation: Following Bezos, most of your work will never be seen by anyone, so take pride in it anyway. Excellence is a habit that builds up from small things into big ones; there is no separate moment when you do 'big things'. Ajay's coda: be humble and self-effacing as a person, but put everything into your work and stand by it.
core_ideas.quote: How you do the small things is how you do the big things.

core_ideas.explanation: Buffett's father's lesson: judge yourself by your own values, not by money, success or what people write about you. Ask whether you were true to your values, told friends the truth when they needed it, and walked your own path. This applies to life and to the company you build.
core_ideas.quote: You know, if you don't score high on your inner scorecard, nothing is worth it.

core_ideas.concept: Business as a Home for Great Thinkers
core_ideas.explanation: Amit, a literature student who once would have been surprised to hear himself say this, argues that many of today's finest thinkers come from business, such as Paul Graham, Naval Ravikant and Peter Thiel. Business is now a route to both making money and changing the world, because a business can only succeed by creating value for people and, at scale, for society.
core_ideas.quote: But I really feel some of our finest thinkers are from the world of business.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: The opening trial. Using cameraman Vaishnav's phrase for Ajay, a bumblebee among the social butterflies (the poet among economists), Amit charges him: 'These allegations have been hurled on you. And in the court of YouTube opinion, Ajay Shah, you must defend yourself.' Ajay, deadpan: 'First you have to kill the joke by explaining it.'
Ajay pleads guilty to one thing: 'Every economist reads Milton Friedman, John Maynard Keynes, Robert Lucas... I study Keynes for language as much as I study Hemingway for language.'
Amit 'translates' the Bollywood number 'Sarkai Lo Khatiya Jaada Lage' into a privatiser's slogan: 'Sarkari Khatiya Private Karo'.

Ajay's admittedly off-topic one-liner, offered because it's 'just too much fun': 'every great idea starts out as a cause and then becomes a movement and then becomes a racket.' Amit: 'That's a brilliant line.'

Kipling's 'What do they know of England who only England know?' and C.L.R. James's cricket version, generalised by Amit to 'What do they know of X who only X know?' as the case for generalist founders.

Imagining a founder dismissing a user who doesn't 'get' his product, Amit casts Ajay as the clueless critic: 'He's a Unix command line user.' He then hastily adds that it's a compliment: 'it's a feature, not a bug.'
Excite, Yahoo and Ask Jeeves, the search engines 'people of our vintage will remember' from the late 1990s, before Google.

The botched call-and-response. Amit: 'Which game do you play, Ajay Shah?' Ajay: 'The hundred year game.' Amit: 'Why can't you just repeat what I said? There's a nice poetry to it.' Take two: 'The long game.' 'That's how I like it. You're following instructions.'
Mike Tyson's 'Everyone has a plan until they get punched in the face', which Ajay supplies when Amit fumbles it, used to frame Bezos's admittedly BS business plan.

On Eric Schmidt's advice to make five-year plans: 'Now you and I, Ajay Shah, are not quite fans of five year plans in an Indian economy context.' Amit's distinction: economies can't be centrally planned, but companies can.

Amit quizzes Ajay on his favourite Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young song, fishing for 'Teach Your Children' to segue into choosing co-founders. Ajay offers 'Helpless' and 'Southern Cross' and calls 'Teach Your Children' 'okay, little cliched'. Amit: 'See, we don't script anything.' The song becomes a running gag: 'Teach your children well, choose your founders well, choose your employees well.'
After Ajay's story about BillDesk's Ajay Kaushal: 'Ajays are awesome. I'm not so sure about Shahs or Amits for that matter.'
Amit on credentials: 'I of course have no credentials, which is despite that Ajay came with me, so he's living the dream. But Ajay has credentials. He is IIT, he has foreign PhD.'
Defending startup founders from Ajay's 'dollar signs' jab: 'You use terms like tech bro disparagingly. Yes, of course, in every community, most people are assholes, that's Sturgeon's law.'
Amit to Ajay, a Britannia board member: 'Are biscuits healthy?' Ajay, diplomatically: 'Some Britannia biscuits are worth eating.'
Narayana Murthy's 70-hour work week. Amit: mandatory, he completely disapproves; voluntary, 'Every hour of my week when I'm not sleeping could be towards that because that is how obsessive I am.'
Apoorva Mehta of Instacart's definition of obsession: the company is the last thing he thinks about at night and the first thing in the morning.
Brian Armstrong's 'Action produces information', carried over from the last episode to link a fixed vision with flexible tactics.
On the Indian habit of pretending to know: ask someone for directions and even if they don't know, they'll confidently point you right, then left, to some paanwala. Amit's coda: 'Not the last part.'
Amit's carve-out from radical truth-telling: 'If your lady love says, Am I looking fat in this dress? Ajay Shah, there is only one answer.'
Professional pride, applied: Amit boasts that the bacon and sourdough he made for the crew the night before 'was the best bacon and sourdough ever made in these climes in which we record.'
